submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole fires retrospectively on the token that names the resolved outcome or resultant state of a preceding episode, such as a return, repetition, departure, recovery, reconciliation, or lesson learned after an earlier action or event. It does not fire on an ordinary ongoing action token, on a plain description of an object, or on a token that merely continues an episode without resolving it.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The school fair was meant to open at ten, and by eight the playground was already busy. Mr Patel backed the van up to the gate and two boys carried boxes of paper cups to the stall by the fence. The bunting had come loose again in the night, and a teacher stood on a chair to tie it to the railing. In the back of the hall, mothers laid out cakes on long tables and argued about which one was better for the raffle. A girl named Priya pulled a box of ribbons out from under the stage and carried it to the face-painting table without being asked. Nobody was in charge of the tombola yet, so the head teacher said, 'Okay, put it next to the swing then,' and the others carried on with what they were doing. The clouds were low and grey, and the wind kept lifting the corner of the tarpaulin, and each time a boy ran to weigh it down with a brick. Children drifted in from the estate in twos and threes, their friends calling to them from the gate, and the queue at the cake stall grew longer. At half past nine the caretaker was still hunting for the key to the storeroom, opening drawers and cupboards and muttering, while the boxes of prizes sat untouched on the grass. A dog slipped its lead and ran between the tables, knocking over a jug of squash, and three adults chased it around the sandpit while the children laughed. Someone said the bouncy castle man was late, and someone else said he was always late, and a woman in a red coat asked whether the face painting cost money. Two boys were throwing a tennis ball against the wall of the dinner hall, and every so often the ball went over the fence and one of them climbed after it and came back with his knees green. The band was tuning up by the bins, the same four notes over and over, and the caretaker was still looking for the key, and the wind was still pulling at the tarpaulin, and nobody had opened the gates.

On the field, the bouncy castle sat half inflated and the man from the hire company was on his phone beside it, and nobody was sure what he was saying. A girl was crawling through the long grass near the sandpit looking for a shoe, and four children got down on their hands and knees to help her. In the kitchen the urn was taking a long time to boil, and the woman in charge of the tea kept lifting the lid and looking inside and putting it down again. The queue at the gate shuffled forward a few steps and then stopped, and the caretaker put his head out of the storeroom door and said he would try the other key, and then went back in.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long passage in the examples' narrative register that keeps every episode open, burying the claimed tokens in spatial, comparative and discourse senses, so the hypothesis predicts no activation anywhere in it.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The gallery's north room holds a collection of nineteenth-century landscape sketches, hung in two rows on walls painted a dull green. The frames are the originals, though the glass has been replaced twice, and the labels are being rewritten this winter. Visitors should start at the left of the doorway and work round the room clockwise; the numbers on the labels follow the same order. A better example of the period hangs above the fireplace, where the light is poor, so the curator has added a small lamp and a note explaining the choice. The two smaller drawings beside the window came to the gallery in a portfolio from a house sale and have never been shown before. Their paper is brown at the edges and the pencil is faded where the sun reached them, and the conservator says that they should be kept out of daylight from now on. On the back of each sheet there is a rough sketch of a hedge and a date, and on one of them a name that nobody has been able to read with any confidence. The room is small, and on busy afternoons the visitors queue at the door and the attendant asks them to move along again so that everyone can see. The benches in the middle are for resting, not for picnics, and the attendant will ask you to take bags off them. Photography is allowed without a flash; tripods are not. In the corner there is a case of tools: a palette knife, three brushes, a small bottle of medium and a rag, arranged to show what a painter of the period would have carried into the field. The list of works is printed on a card by the door, and a copy in large type is available from the desk on request. The exhibition continues until March, and the room closes at half past four, half an hour before the rest of the building. The stairs down to the shop are narrow and the handrail is worn smooth in the middle, and the attendant asks visitors to keep to the right. A short film about the restoration runs every twenty minutes in the anteroom, and the seats there are hard and the sound is quiet, and most people stand at the back until it finishes. The gallery is free to enter, and the room is often full on wet afternoons, when the coaches arrive from the coast and the corridor by the shop is crowded with children in matching coats. The curator asks that groups of more than ten telephone in advance, and that teachers keep their pupils together near the fireplace, where there is more space. The sketches themselves are small, no larger than a postcard, and the pencil marks are faint, so the labels are set low and the light is kept dim. A bench by the door holds a folder of photographs of the same views taken in recent years, and visitors are welcome to leaf through it and to write a comment in the book beside it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long descriptive catalogue, the plain-object-description case the hypothesis excludes, carrying 'back', 'better' and 'again' only in the wrong senses with no episode that resolves.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The little terrier had slipped out through the gap in the fence on Saturday morning, and by lunchtime the whole street knew she was missing. Anna walked to the recreation ground and called her name along the hedge, then down to the canal and along the towpath as far as the lock. A man fishing under the bridge said he had seen a small brown dog heading towards the allotments an hour before, so she cut across the field behind the garages and asked two boys on bicycles whether they had noticed anything. They had not, but they promised to keep an eye out and rode off towards the main road. At the allotments an old woman watering her beans let Anna look inside the shed and behind the compost heap, and then made her sit down and drink a glass of water while she telephoned her own daughter, who knew everyone on the allotment committee. The afternoon went on like that: telephone calls, a walk around the pond, a description given to the man at the corner shop, a poster taped to the noticeboard by the church with a photograph and a telephone number cut from the bottom. Anna's mother drove the streets with the window down, stopping every few minutes to listen. By six o'clock the light was fading and the rain had started, and Anna sat on the doorstep with her coat still on, too miserable to go inside. Her mother brought out a cup of tea and sat beside her and said nothing.

Then, at twenty past six, there was a scratching at the gate, and a small wet shape pushed through the gap and trotted up the path with its tail low and its ears flat. Anna was off the step before her mother could speak. The terrier was muddy and thin and shivering, and there was a cut on one paw, but she was home at last, and she stood in the kitchen while Anna wrapped her in a towel and cried into her neck. The vet's van came at seven, and the young woman who got out of it looked at the paw on the kitchen table and said it would heal cleanly with a wash and a bandage. Anna's father made toast, and nobody mentioned the posters still taped to the noticeboard by the church or the description given to the man at the corner shop, and the terrier slept in the basket by the radiator with her bandaged paw hanging over the edge.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long narrative in which the search runs for hundreds of tokens and the resultant state ('she was home at last') lands deep in the passage, testing whether the pole follows a resolved outcome across long context.
